segments.translation: [Bhusukupāda]{p-bhusuku} sets forth that same meaning in the [twilight language]{sandhya-bhasa} of the [mouse]{mouse}:
segments.note: Munidatta introduces the song as [Bhusukupāda]{p-bhusuku} setting forth 'that same meaning', as in the comment before, in the [twilight language]{sandhya-bhasa} of the [mouse]{mouse} (cp.21.m1). The Tibetan calls the poet 'du shes gsum pa'i zhabs, 'the master of the three notions', translating his name rather than transcribing it.

flags.note: The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) names the poet 'du shes gsum pa'i zhabs, 'the master of the three notions', rendering the name Bhusuku by a sense (as in its heading of the song) instead of transcribing it. Otherwise it agrees: don de nyid byi ba dgongs pa'i skad kyis ... gsungs te, 'spoke that very meaning in the intentional language of the mouse'.
The segment does not say what 'that same meaning' (tam evārtham) is; Munidatta uses the phrase to join a song to the teaching of the one before (cp.21.m1), here presumably the comment on song 20.

segments.translit:
niśi āndhīrītyādi| muṣnātīti mūṣaka[ḥ] sandhyāvacane cittapavanaḥ boddhavyaḥ| nisi prajñā karmmāṅganā vā boddhavyā| tasyā[ḥ] karmmāṅganāyā vicitrādikṣaṇe kāyānandādivyāpāradvāreṇa kuliśāravindasaṃyoge bodhicittāmṛtāsvādāhāraṃ sa eva mūṣaka[ḥ] cittapavanaḥ svayaṃ karoti| tasmin viramānandaṃ dakṣiṇe śrīgurumukhalabdhopāyena drutaṃ tasya niḥsvabhāvīkaraṇaṃ bhavati| tat kurvvato bālayoginas tena saṃsāracakre yātāyātaṃ dvayākāran na truṭyati cittañ ca na śobhate|
tathā cāgama[ḥ]
dvayākāreṇa tyāgaprakaṭapaṭusaṃvittisubhage
ghanānandotkīrṇe prabalarasapūrṇāmbaratale|
sphuṭan nānākārair upacitaśametāntaragatai-
r idaṃ tantrai[ru]ktaṃ layam iva gataṃ bhāti manasi||
segments.translation:
'In the dark [night]{night}…' and so on. It steals (muṣṇāti), so it is a [mouse]{mouse} (mūṣaka): in [twilight language]{sandhya-bhasa} it is to be understood as the [mind-wind]{cittapavana}. The [night]{night} (nisi) is to be understood as [wisdom]{prajna} or as the [karmamudrā]{karmamudra}. In that [karmamudrā]{karmamudra}'s moments beginning with [vicitra]{vicitra}, through the activity of the [joys]{ananda} beginning with the joy of the body, in the union of [vajra]{vajra} and [lotus]{lotus}, that very [mouse]{mouse}, the [mind-wind]{cittapavana}, itself makes a meal of the taste of the [nectar]{amrta} of [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta}. In it, at the moment of the [joy of cessation]{viramananda}, it is quickly made [without intrinsic nature]{nihsvabhava} by the means received from the mouth of the glorious [guru]{guru}. For the [novice yogin]{balayogin} who does that, therefore, [coming and going]{coming-and-going} in the wheel of [saṃsāra]{samsara}, in its dual form, is not cut off, and his [mind]{citta} does not shine. And so the [scripture]{agama}:
'In the expanse of a [sky]{gagana} lovely with keen awareness made plain by giving up the dual form,
carved from dense [joy]{ananda} and brimming with a powerful essence,
unfolding in manifold forms that have gathered calm and gone within,
this, which the tantras speak of, shines in the [mind]{citta} as though dissolved.'
segments.note: Munidatta reads the mouse, 'the stealer', as the [mind-wind]{cittapavana}, and the night as [wisdom]{prajna} or the [karmamudrā]{karmamudra} (cp.21.m2). In union the mind-wind itself feeds on the nectar of [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta}; at the [joy of cessation]{viramananda} the guru's means quickly makes it without intrinsic nature. For the novice yogin 'who does that' (Tibetan: who lacks it), coming and going continues.

equations.en: the mind-wind (cittapavana), so called because it steals (muṣṇāti)

citations.quoted: dvayākāreṇa tyāgaprakaṭapaṭusaṃvittisubhage / ghanānandotkīrṇe prabalarasapūrṇāmbaratale / sphuṭan nānākārair upacitaśametāntaragatair / idaṃ tantrair uktaṃ layam iva gataṃ bhāti manasi

flags.note: Munidatta's lemma reads niśi āndhīrī where the song has nisia andhārī (cp.21.m2); translated with the draft's 'In the dark night'.

Where the Sanskrit has 'the night is to be understood as wisdom or as the karmāṅganā' (prajñā karmmāṅganā vā), the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has no 'or' and a single phrase, shes rab las kyi phyag rgya'i yan lag, 'the limb of the wisdom action seal', taking aṅganā as aṅga, 'limb'; so too de'i las kyi yan lag, 'her action-limb', for tasyāḥ karmāṅganāyāḥ. It also has 'mind and wind' (sems dang rlung) for cittapavana, and 'the nectar food' (bdud rtsi'i zas) without 'taste' (āsvāda).
karmāṅganā, literally 'action-woman', is rendered with the glossary's 'karmamudrā', under which the glossary files this form. See questions.
The genitive tasyāḥ karmāṅganāyāḥ, 'of that karmamudrā', may go with 'the moments beginning with vicitra' (so translated) or with 'the union of vajra and lotus'.

tasmin viramānandaṃ dakṣiṇe does not construe ('in it, the joy of cessation, in the right/south'). The Tibetan de la khyad par gyi dga' ba'i skad cig la, 'in it, at the moment of the joy of cessation', supports reading viramānandakṣaṇe; I translate that. The printed anusvāra and da look like scribal corruption.

tasya, 'its', in 'its being made without intrinsic nature' may refer to the mouse, the mind-wind (matching the refrain's 'kill the mouse'), or to bodhicitta; the Tibetan (de'i rang bzhin med par bya'o) is equally open. The Tibetan also has 'the means heard (thos pa) from the glorious guru's mouth' for 'received' (labdha), and 'is to be made' for 'takes place'.

tat kurvato bālayoginaḥ, 'for the novice yogin who does that', is translated as printed. If 'that' is the making without intrinsic nature just described, the sentence contradicts itself and a negative may be lost (tad akurvataḥ, 'who does not do that'); if 'that' is the mouse's meal taken without the guru's means, it stands. The Tibetan points to the negative: byis pa'i rnal 'byor pas de dang bral bar byas nas, 'when the novice yogin has become separated from that'. Its quotation of the refrain is also negative (cp.21.2a ma bsad, 'not killing'; cp.21.2b ma bkag na, 'if not stopped').

For 'his mind does not shine' (cittañ ca na śobhate) the Tibetan has sems sdug bsngal bar byed, 'makes the mind suffer', as if reading a form of śuc, 'grieve'. It takes dvayākāra as 'the two aspects' (rnam pa gnyis), that is, going and coming, which is why I use the neutral 'dual form'.

Verse line 1: the verse is in Śikhariṇī, and lines 2 to 4 scan, but dvayākāreṇa tyāga° gives line 1 eighteen syllables, and the instrumental does not construe. The compound dvayākāratyāgaprakaṭapaṭusaṃvittisubhage scans exactly and matches the Tibetan rnam pa gnyis spong, 'abandoning the two aspects'. I translate the compound.

Verse line 3: upacitaśametāntaragataiḥ is obscure. I take it as 'that have gathered calm (upacita-śama-ita) and gone within'; śameta could also stand for sameta, 'joined together'. The Tibetan has sems 'khrugs zhi ba de nang song ba, 'the agitated mind calmed, gone within'. In line 2, for ghanānandotkīrṇe, 'carved from dense joy', it has dga' bas khyab pa, 'pervaded by joy'.

Verse line 4: for idaṃ tantrair uktaṃ, 'this, which the tantras speak of' (the syllable ru is Shastri's restoration), the Tibetan has de nyid 'jig rten gsum po thim gyur, 'that very threefold world dissolved', as if its manuscript had a form of trailokya, 'the three worlds', in the damaged place. For bhāti manasi, 'shines in the mind', it has yid ni gsal bar byed, 'makes the mind clear'.

segments.translit:
dvitīyapadena mūṣakacittasya vyavahāro 'nuvarṇṇyate—
bhavetyādi| bhavatīti kṛtvā bhavaṃ svakāyaṃ vidārayati prakṛticāñcalyatayā sa evaṃ cittaṃ mūṣako 'nyathābhāvaṃ kurute| gatīti tiryyaṅnarakādidurgatipātañ ca| svayam eva utpādayati| ataś cittamūṣakasya prakṛtidoṣam ākalayya bho yogin prasādāptopadeśena tasya bhāvāropaṇaṃ na kariṣyasīti|
segments.translation: With the second [verse]{pada} the behaviour of the [mouse]{mouse}-[mind]{citta} is described. 'Existence…' and so on. Because it comes to be (bhavati), [existence]{bhava} (bhava) is one's own [body]{body}: this it tears apart through its natural restlessness. That very [mind]{citta}-[mouse]{mouse} brings about alteration. 'Holes' (gatī) means: it itself also brings about the fall into the [lower realms]{durgati} (durgati) of animals, the hells and the rest. Therefore, O [yogi]{yogi}, having considered the [fault of nature]{prakrtidosa} of the [mind]{citta}-[mouse]{mouse}, you will make no [imputation]{aropa} of real existence upon it, through the [instruction]{upadesa} obtained by grace.
segments.note: Munidatta reads the couplet as the mind-mouse's behaviour (cp.21.m3): in its natural restlessness it tears apart [existence]{bhava}, which he explains as one's own body, and he takes the holes (gātī) as gati, 'destiny': the mind itself brings about the fall into the [lower realms]{durgati}. Seeing this fault, the yogi must not impute real existence to it.

equations.en: one's own body (so called because it comes to be, bhavati)
the fall into the lower realms, the animal realm, the hells and the rest, which the mind-mouse itself brings about (read as gati, 'destiny')

flags.note: The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) opens rkang pa gnyis pas byi ba sems kyi tha snyad kyi rjes su bsngags pa gsungs te, 'with the second verse he spoke the praise of the convention of the mouse-mind', taking vyavahāra as 'convention' (tha snyad) and anuvarṇyate as 'is praised'; I take them as 'behaviour' and 'is described'.

prakṛticāñcalyatayā, 'through its natural restlessness', may close the first clause (so translated) or open the next; the Tibetan attaches it to the next (rang bzhin gyis g.yo ba de yis ... gzhan gyi ngo bor byed).

sa evaṃ cittaṃ mūṣako is apparently for sa eva cittamūṣako, 'that very mind-mouse', as the Tibetan de nyid sems kyi byi ba confirms. For anyathābhāvaṃ kurute, 'brings about alteration', the Tibetan has gzhan gyi ngo bor byed, 'makes it into the nature of another'.

Where Munidatta cites the song's gātī, 'holes', as gatī and hears gati, 'destiny' (cp.21.m3), the Tibetan comment instead glosses rtsig pa, 'wall', the word of its own line ('bores through a wall'); the gloss, the fall into the lower realms (ngan 'gro), is the same.
The Tibetan has man ngag thos pa de yis, 'by the instruction heard', without 'grace' (prasāda), and bgrangs nas, 'having counted up', for ākalayya, 'having considered'.
bhāva in bhāvāropaṇa may be 'real existence' (so translated) or 'a thing'; the Tibetan has dngos por sgro btags pa, 'imputing it as a thing'.

segments.translit:
tṛtīyapadena tasya svarūpam āha—
kāletyādi| saṃvṛttibodhicittaṃ dunāśakatvena sa eva cittamūṣakaḥ kālaḥ| tasya piṇḍagrāhānubhede vicāreṇa bho yogin varṇopalambhopadeśo na vidyate| gaganam iti gurusampradāyāt mahāsukhakamalavanaṃ gatvā punar āgatya paramārthabodhicittamadhupānāsvādaṃ karoti|
tathā ca paradarśane| mīnanāthaḥ—
kahanti guru paramārthera bāṭa
karmmakuraṅga samādhika pāṭa|
kamala bikasila kahiha ṇa jamarā
kamalamadhu pibibi dhoke na bhamarā||
segments.translation:
With the third [verse]{pada} he states its [true nature]{svarupa}. 'Black…' and so on. Because it destroys the [moon]{moon} of [conventional]{samvrti} [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta}, that very [mind]{citta}-[mouse]{mouse} is [Death]{kala} (kāla). When it is examined in [piṇḍagrāha and anubheda]{pindagraha-anubheda}, O [yogi]{yogi}, there is no [instruction]{upadesa} on apprehending any colour. 'Sky' means: through the [guru's lineage]{guru-sampradaya} it goes to the [lotus grove]{nalinivana} of [great bliss]{mahasukha}, comes back again, and relishes drinking the [honey]{honey} of [ultimate]{paramartha} [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta}. And so, in another school, [Mīnanātha]{p-minanatha}:
'The [guru]{guru} tells of the [road]{road} of the [ultimate]{paramartha},
the [deer]{deer} of karma, the [pāṭa]{pata} of [samādhi]{samadhi}.
The [lotus]{lotus} has opened: do not tell Yama.
Having drunk the [honey]{honey} of the [lotus]{lotus}, the bee is not deceived.'
segments.note: Munidatta reads the black (kāla) mouse as [Death]{kala}, destroyer of the moon of conventional [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta}; the Tibetan makes it Rāhu (cp.21.m4). Examined in [piṇḍagrāha and anubheda]{pindagraha-anubheda}, it shows no colour (the Tibetan names none). For 'sky', it goes by the guru's lineage to the [lotus grove]{nalinivana} of great bliss, returning to drink ultimate bodhicitta's honey in place of amaṇa dhāṇa.

equations.en: Death: the mind-mouse, as destroyer of the moon of conventional bodhicitta
going through the guru's lineage to the lotus grove of great bliss and coming back (a paraphrase after 'gaganam iti')

citations.quoted: kahanti guru paramārthera bāṭa / karmmakuraṅga samādhika pāṭa / kamala bikasila kahiha ṇa jamarā / kamalamadhu pibibi dhoke na bhamarā
citations.work: Old Bengali verse ascribed by Munidatta to Mīnanātha, quoted 'in another school' (paradarśane); no work named (cp.21.m4)

flags.note: saṃvṛttibodhicittaṃ dunāśakatvena does not construe: dunāśaka is not a word, and the accusative hangs. I read saṃvṛttibodhicittendunāśakatvena, 'because it destroys the moon (indu) of conventional bodhicitta', with the Tibetan kun rdzob byang chub kyi sems kyi zla ba 'joms pa nyid kyis, 'by its destroying the moon of conventional bodhicitta'. Without the emendation: 'because it destroys conventional bodhicitta'.

For kāla the Tibetan comment has sgra gcan, Rāhu, the eclipse demon, as does the Tibetan of the song line (cp.21.4a byi ba sgra gcan), though its lemma is nag po, 'black'. Compare cp.01.m2, where Munidatta himself identifies Kāla with Rāhu, who swallows the moon of conventional bodhicitta.

The lemma kāla takes up the song's kalā, 'black' (the draft's 'black mouse'), and the gloss turns on kāla as time, the destroyer (cp.21.m4). I use the glossary's 'Death' and add kāla in parentheses so the play stays visible. See questions.

For tasya piṇḍagrāhānubhede vicāreṇa ... varṇopalambhopadeśo na vidyate the Tibetan has de'i phung po za bas dbye bas rnam par dpyod pas ... gdams pa thob pa la med pa'o, 'examining it by division, by eating the heap, ... for one who has obtained the instruction it is not there', as if reading piṇḍagrāsa, 'eating a lump', and with no word for colour.

varṇopalambhopadeśo na vidyate is literally 'there is no instruction on the apprehension of colour'; it may mean 'no colour is taught as something to apprehend'. Either way it answers the song's 'has no colour'.

'Sky' means (gaganam iti) is followed by a paraphrase, not a noun, so it is not explicit whether the sky is the lotus grove of great bliss or the going there. The honey of ultimate bodhicitta stands where the song has the mouse graze on amaṇa dhāṇa; those words are not glossed. The Tibetan has 'from the guru's instruction' (bla ma'i man ngag las) for 'through the guru's lineage'.
For 'in another school' (paradarśane) the Tibetan makes Mīnanātha 'a holder of an outsider's view' (phyi rol gyi lta ba pa).

Mīnanātha's Old Bengali verse is uncertain. Line 2 (karmmakuraṅga samādhika pāṭa) is rendered word for word; pāṭa may be a bar or door-panel (the Tibetan has sgo glegs). jamarā is taken as Yama ('do not tell Yama'), and dhoke na as 'is not deceived' (compare Bengali dhokā, 'deceit'). The Tibetan differs throughout: 'the guru spoke the ultimate, the stages of the path (lam gyi rim pa, as if krama for karma), samādhi with door-panels; the lotus opened, it is said, and there is no king of death (gshin rje'i rgyal med); the bee drinks the lotus honey', with no deer and nothing for dhoke na.

segments.translit:
caturthapadena vajragurumāhātmyam āha—
tāva setyādi| cittamūṣako 'yaṃ tāvad eva mohamānenonnato bhavati| yāvat sadguruvacanayantrasannidhānaṃ na bhavati| bho yogin tasmāt gurau praṇidhānam ārabhyatām iti|
tathā ca sarahapādāḥ—
yasya prasādakiraṇair ityādi|
segments.translation: With the fourth [verse]{pada} he states the greatness of the [vajra]{vajra} [guru]{guru}. 'Till then…' and so on. This [mind]{citta}-[mouse]{mouse} stays puffed up with [delusion]{moha} and [pride]{mana-pride} only as long as the device of the true [guru]{guru}'s word is not at hand. Therefore, O [yogi]{yogi}, devote yourself to the [guru]{guru}. And so [Saraha]{p-saraha}: 'By the rays of whose grace…' and so on.
segments.note: Munidatta reads the couplet as the greatness of the vajra [guru]{guru} (cp.21.m5): the mind-mouse stays puffed up with [delusion]{moha} and [pride]{mana-pride} until the device of the true guru's word is at hand, so the yogi should devote himself to the guru. The Tibetan adds that the mouse first goes to the lotus grove.

citations.work: a verse of Saraha, named by Munidatta (cp.21.m5) and cited by its opening words only; perhaps the verse in praise of the true guru that the glossary records at cp.01.m3

flags.note: Munidatta's lemma is tāva se (cp.21.m5) where the song has tabase; translated with the draft's 'Till then'.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) construes the paraphrase differently: sems kyi byi ba 'di de srid pa de nyid rmongs pa dang nga rgyal zhi bar mi 'gyur ro/ /gang gi tshe chu skyes kyi tshal du song nas bla ma dam pa'i gsung gi 'khrul 'khor gyis nyams su myong bar byed do, 'for so long this mind-mouse's delusion and pride are not pacified; when, having gone to the lotus grove, it has experience through the device of the true guru's word'. The Sanskrit has 'puffed up' (unnata) and no lotus grove.

For 'let devotion to the guru be undertaken' (gurau praṇidhānam ārabhyatām), translated 'devote yourself to the guru', the Tibetan has bla ma'i bzhed pa btsal bar bya'o, 'the guru's wish is to be sought'.
yantra, 'device, instrument', can also mean a restraint or fetter, and for a mouse a trap may be in view, though the text does not say so. The Tibetan has 'khrul 'khor, 'device'.

segments.translit:
pañcamapadena cittamūṣakasya svarūpam āha—
jabem ityādi| yasmin samaye sahajānandacittamūṣakasyācāraḥ| aham iti| pratyāropayatā truṭyati| tasmin samaye saṃsārabandhanaṃ tasya| sphiṭam iti|
yathā cāgamaḥ—
saṃsāro 'sti na tattvatas tanubhṛtāṃ bandhasya cātraiva kā
bandho yatra na yāti kācid a(ta)thā muktasya muktakriyaḥ|
mithyāropakṛto 'tha rajjubhujagacchāyāpiśācabhramo
mā kiñcit tyaja mā gṛhāṇa vilasa sve stho yathāvasthitaḥ|| 21||
segments.translation:
With the fifth [verse]{pada} he states the [true nature]{svarupa} of the [mind]{citta}-[mouse]{mouse}. 'When…' and so on. At the time when there is the roaming of the [mind]{citta}-[mouse]{mouse} of [innate joy]{sahajananda}, the [imputation]{aropa} 'I' is cut off; at that time his [bond]{bandhana} of [saṃsāra]{samsara} 'breaks' (sphiṭa). As the [scripture]{agama} says:
'In [reality]{tattva} there is no [saṃsāra]{samsara} for the embodied; and what [bond]{bandhana} is there right here,
a [bond]{bandhana} into which no one goes? Unreal, too, is the freeing of the one who is free.
It is made by false [imputation]{aropa}: the error of a snake in a rope, of a goblin in a shadow.
Give up nothing, take hold of nothing; play, at rest in yourself, just as you are.'
segments.note: Munidatta reads the last couplet as the mind-mouse's true nature (cp.21.m6): when the mind-mouse of [innate joy]{sahajananda} roams, the [imputation]{aropa} 'I' is cut off and the bond of saṃsāra breaks (the syntax is uncertain; the Tibetan agrees in sense). The verse he quotes calls bondage false imputation, a rope taken for a snake: give up nothing, grasp nothing.

citations.quoted: saṃsāro 'sti na tattvatas tanubhṛtāṃ bandhasya cātraiva kā / bandho yatra na yāti kācid a(ta)thā muktasya muktakriyaḥ / mithyāropakṛto 'tha rajjubhujagacchāyāpiśācabhramo / mā kiñcit tyaja mā gṛhāṇa vilasa sve stho yathāvasthitaḥ

flags.note: The syntax of yasmin samaye sahajānandacittamūṣakasyācāraḥ | aham iti | pratyāropayatā truṭyati is uncertain. I follow Shastri's punctuation and the Tibetan: 'when the mind-mouse of innate joy roams, the imputation "I" is cut off' (Tibetan: gang gi tshe lhan cig skyes pa'i dga' ba la sems kyi byi ba rgyu ba'o/ /nga zhes rkyen gyis brtags pa rgyun gcod pa'o, 'when the mind-mouse roams in innate joy; the "I" imputed by conditions has its stream cut'). As printed, pratyāropayatā is an instrumental participle, 'by one who imputes', which gives the alternative 'when the roaming of the mind-mouse of innate joy is cut off by one who imputes "I"', closer to the song's own 'when the roaming is cut off'. The Tibetan rkyen, 'condition', suggests its translators read pratyaya.
ācāra, usually 'conduct', here takes up the song's cā, which the draft renders 'roaming'; the Tibetan has rgyu ba, 'moving, roaming'.
Where Munidatta renders the song's phiṭaa, 'breaks', as sphiṭa (cp.21.m6), the Tibetan has 'khor bar 'ching ba gcod pa, 'the binding into saṃsāra is cut', and nothing for tasya, 'his'.

Verse line 2: Shastri prints kācida(ta)thā. The Śārdūlavikrīḍita metre needs kācid atathā, which I take as 'unreal'; muktasya muktakriyaḥ is loosely construed as 'the freeing of the one who is free', and the line as a whole is uncertain. The Tibetan read tathā: de bzhin grol byas grol bar bya, 'likewise, having freed, one is to be freed'; for 'a bond into which no one goes' it has 'ga' zhig gang du 'chi med 'gro, 'where does anyone go deathless'. It groups 'of the embodied' with bondage (lus 'dzin 'ching ba 'dir gang las, 'from what is the bondage of the embodied here?'). Lines 3 and 4 agree.

proposals.definition: Honey (Sanskrit and Old Bengali madhu; Tibetan sbrang rtsi), the sweet juice bees gather from flowers, above all the lotus. Munidatta has the mind-mouse drink 'the honey of ultimate bodhicitta' after going to the lotus grove of great bliss, and quotes Mīnanātha on the bee drinking the honey of the opened lotus (cp.21.m4).

symbolicReadings.referent: ultimate bodhicitta: 'the honey of ultimate bodhicitta' (paramārthabodhicittamadhu), which the mind-mouse drinks after going, through the guru's lineage, to the lotus grove of great bliss and returning

proposals.rationale: Honey recurs in Munidatta's comments: the honey of the uṣṇīṣa lotus (cp.04.m3, now filed under the lotus entry), the honey-drink of knowledge in song 16 (see the entry for 'drunk'), and twice at cp.21.m4. It is a different word from nectar (amṛta) and liquor (āsava), and 'honey' already appears in never-in-line lists, so an entry keeps the rendering consistent.

questions: cp.21.m2: Munidatta's word for the partner is karmāṅganā, 'action-woman' (cp.21.m2), which the glossary files under karmamudra, so I wrote 'karmamudrā'. Should 'action-woman' be added as a variant, so that the translation can keep his word?

cp.21.m2: 'tat kurvato bālayoginaḥ', 'for the novice yogin who does that' (cp.21.m2), is translated as printed. The Tibetan comment ('when the novice yogin has become separated from that') and the Tibetan quotation of the refrain both point to a lost negative (tad akurvataḥ, 'who does not do that'). Emend, or keep the printed text with the flag?

cp.21.2a-2b (the draft, outside this task): the Tibetan quotation of the refrain is negative and conditional: kye'i rnal 'byor rlung byi ma bsad cing / gang gis 'gro dang 'ong ba ma bkag na, 'O yogi, if you do not kill the wind-mouse, and coming and going is not stopped by it'. Munidatta's paraphrase likewise ends 'is not cut off' (cp.21.m2). The draft lines may want a witness note.

cp.21.m4: I emended 'saṃvṛttibodhicittaṃ dunāśakatvena' to 'saṃvṛttibodhicittendunāśakatvena', 'because it destroys the moon of conventional bodhicitta' (cp.21.m4), on the strength of the Tibetan zla ba 'joms pa. Accept, or translate 'because it destroys conventional bodhicitta' and leave du- unexplained?

cp.21.m4: the glossary's 'Death' for kāla hides the play on the song's kalā, 'black', which is the point of Munidatta's gloss (cp.21.m4). I kept 'Death' and added '(kāla)'. Would 'Kāla' or 'time' serve better here?

cp.21.m6: which construal of 'aham iti pratyāropayatā truṭyati' (cp.21.m6)? I followed the Tibetan, 'when the mind-mouse of innate joy roams, the imputation "I" is cut off'. The printed instrumental participle would give 'the roaming is cut off by one who imputes "I"', closer to the song's own line.

cp.21.m4: Mīnanātha's verse (cp.21.m4) is the least certain passage. Is jamarā Yama (the Tibetan has gshin rje'i rgyal, 'king of death')? Is 'do not tell' (kahiha ṇa) right, or should it be 'say: there is no Yama', nearer the Tibetan? Is dhoke na 'is not deceived'? And is karmakuraṅga, 'the deer of karma', right against the Tibetan's 'stages of the path'?

cp.21.m5: Saraha's verse is cited only by its opening words, yasya prasādakiraṇaiḥ (cp.21.m5). The glossary records Munidatta quoting Saraha in praise of the true guru at cp.01.m3; if it is the same verse, the edition could cross-refer to it.

Proposal 'honey' (madhu): it occurs at cp.04.m3, in song 16 and twice at cp.21.m4 (all Munidatta's comments), and 'honey' already sits in never-in-line lists. Is it worth an entry, or should it stay unmarked?
